system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 11 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2177-11-03 04:17:00 to 2177-11-13 17:45:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted with groin pain and an empty Foley catheter bag, which resolved upon sitting up. Evaluation revealed no urinary tract infection despite a positive initial urinalysis; repeat testing and culture indicated colonization rather than infection, so antibiotics were avoided. Left leg redness and swelling were assessed with ultrasound, which ruled out DVT, and findings were consistent with stasis dermatitis. His chronic right heel pressure ulcer showed no signs of infection and required only continued wound care. He remained stable throughout the admission, with no evidence of sepsis or cardiac decompensation. Blood cultures remained negative. He was discharged home with services, on unchanged home medications except for an increase in lisinopril to 5 mg daily, and with clear instructions on catheter care and when to seek medical attention.
problems: Mechanical complication due to urethral (indwelling) catheter
Urinary catheterization as the cause of abnormal reaction of patient, or of later complication, without mention of misadventure at time of procedure
Hypertrophy (benign) of prostate with urinary obstruction and other lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS)
Diabetes mellitus without mention of complication, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled
Coronary atherosclerosis of unspecified type of vessel, native or graft

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  ___ male patient with right lower quadrant tenderness. 
The patient's past history is significant for hypotonic bladder necessitating
chronic indwelling Foley catheter since ___, complicated by drug resistant
UTIs.

COMPARISON:  CT of the abdomen and pelvis ___.

TECHNIQUE:  Multidetector CT imaging of the abdomen and pelvis was obtained
after the administration of 130 cc of Omnipaque intravenous contrast. 
Sagittal and coronal reformations were performed and reviewed.

FINDINGS:  Mild pleural calcifications are seen bilaterally, likely
representing prior asbestos exposure.  Minimal atelectasis is seen in the
dependent portion of the left lower lobe.  Trace left pleural effusion is
seen. The imaged portion of the heart demonstrates extensive coronary
calcifications in the coronary arteries and aortic annulus, unchanged since
prior study.

The liver enhances homogeneously, without focal lesions.  There is no intra-
or extra-hepatic biliary dilatation.  Minimal hyperdense material layering in
the gallbladder, likely represents tiny gallstones.  The adrenal glands, and
spleen are normal.  There is diffuse fatty atrophy of the pancreas, unchanged
since the prior study.  Again seen is an enhancing mass in the upper pole of
the right kidney measuring 3.8 x 3.4 x 3.4 cm, stable since the prior study
where it measured 3.4 x 3.2 x 3.1 cm.  Subcentimeter hypodensity in the left
kidney, is too small to characterize.  No hydronephrosis or new concerning
renal masses are seen.  A small hypodensity secondary to a previously ruptured
right renal cortical cyst (2:41) in the lower pole of the right kidney is
unchanged.  The abdominal aorta has moderate-to-severe atherosclerotic
calcification extending to both iliac arteries, without aneurysmal dilation. 
The stomach is normal.  The assessment of the small and large bowel loops is
somewhat limited by patient motion.  The appendix is not definitely visualized
but no secondary signs of appendicitis are detected.  However, motion at this
level limits further evaluation.  No intra-abdominal free fluid or air is
seen.

CT OF THE PELVIS WITHOUT INTRAVENOUS CONTRAST:  There is symmetric wall
thickening of the urinary bladder, likely secondary to prior UTIs.  A Foley
catheter is seen within the bladder.  Again seen is moderate enlargement of
the prostate gland measuring 5.9 x 4.9 cm.  The rectum and sigmoid colon are
unremarkable.  There is moderate fecal loading throughout the entire colon. 
No pelvic lymphadenopathy or free fluid is seen.  Bilateral small
fat-containing inguinal hernias are seen.

BONES AND SOFT TISSUES:  No bone lesions suspicious for infection or
malignancy are detected.  Again seen are extensive degenerative changes in the
lumbar spine, worse at L4-L5 and L5-S1 levels with extensive facet
arthropathy.  There is mild grade 1 anterolisthesis of L4 on L5.  Mild
compression of the anterior aspect of the L1 vertebral body, is unchanged.
  
IMPRESSION:
1.  The appendix is not definitely visualized.  No secondary signs of
appendicitis are seen.  The presence of motion at this level limits further
evaluation.
2.  Enhancing right upper pole renal mass, concerning for renal cell
carcinoma, stable since the recent prior study of ___.
3.  Cholelithiasis.
4.  Moderate fecal loading throughout the entire colon.
5.  Stable mild compression of L1 vertebral body, unchanged.
6.  Extensive coronary arterial calcification and aortic annular
calcification.

TECHNIQUE:  Multidetector CT imaging of the head was obtained wit  intravenous

FINDINGS:  There is no evidence of intracranial hemorrhage, edema, masses or
mass effect.  The gray-white matter differentiation is normal.  The ventricles
and sulci are moderately enlarged, consistent with moderate involutional
changes.  The basal cisterns are normal.  Again seen is a partially calcified

is seen in the adjacent parenchyma.  Moderate calcifications are seen in the

The imaged paranasal sinuses and mastoid air cells are clear.  Bilateral

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. ___. I’m Dr. ___. You’re in the hospital because your daughter noticed you were confused and having tremors last night. Do you remember coming in?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I… I remember my daughter was worried. I felt hot and shaky. I kept grabbing the air like I was falling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, she said you were oriented but confused. We’ve done some tests. Your CT scan of the head showed no stroke or bleeding. There’s a small stable meningioma, but it’s not new or causing this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Meningioma? Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a benign brain tumor we’ve seen before on prior scans. It hasn’t changed and isn’t causing your symptoms. We’re more focused on why you had confusion and tremors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had tremors before. My neurologist calls it myoclonus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. You’re followed for myoclonic tremors. But the confusion is new. We checked your blood work—no infection, no electrolyte problems, no low blood sugar.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had a lot of UTIs because of my catheter. Could that be it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We thought about that. Your urine looked abnormal, but the culture showed mixed bacteria—likely contamination, not a real infection. So we don’t think it’s a UTI this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what caused the confusion?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think it’s delirium—temporary confusion. It can happen in older adults, especially with changes in meds or underlying conditions. We’ve consulted geriatrics to review your medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I take a lot of pills… Celexa, Cymbalta, tolterodine…

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Tolterodine and Celexa can contribute to confusion in some patients. The geriatrics team recommended stopping both. We’ll increase your Cymbalta to 30 mg daily instead.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that help the tremors?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Cymbalta may help with nerve-related tremors and mood. We’ll also adjust your trazodone for sleep—up to 100 mg at night if needed, but not more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… and my blood pressure? I’ve been feeling a bit dizzy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood pressure has been low—systolic in the 90s to 110s. We’ve stopped lisinopril and furosemide for now. You’re still on metoprolol, which is safe for your heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had heart surgery years ago… triple bypass.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and we’re keeping your aspirin and atorvastatin to protect your heart. Your CT showed heavy calcium in the arteries, so those meds are important.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my kidney? I’ve had that mass for years.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The renal mass is still there, but it hasn’t changed. Urology is following it. No treatment needed now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my eyes? They’ve been crusty.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have conjunctivitis—likely from poor eye hygiene. We’ve started erythromycin eye gel. It should clear up in a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And this rash on my face?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Seborrheic dermatitis. We’re using triamcinolone cream. It’s already improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re much more alert today. Your labs are stable. The delirium seems to be resolving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel like myself again. No more confusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. We’ll keep monitoring. Your catheter is fine—no signs of infection. We’ll continue your usual bowel regimen for constipation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had trouble with that for years.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve kept docusate, senna, and polyethylene glycol. That should help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat labs look good. White count is normal, kidney function stable. We’re confident you don’t have an infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge to an extended care facility for a short stay. You’ll get help with rehab and monitoring before going home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your eye drainage is much better. Keep using the gel for one more day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s less crusty. My face rash is better too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll send the triamcinolone cream home with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood pressure is stable without lisinopril or furosemide. We’ll keep it that way for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No dizziness anymore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Your heart is doing well. Continue aspirin and atorvastatin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve scheduled follow-up with your new primary care doctor, neurology, and urology.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m switching doctors?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, transitioning to a new PCP in ___. They’ll get all your records.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing so well. We’re finalizing your discharge plan for tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready. Thank you for helping me feel clear again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today we’ll go over your discharge meds. We stopped Celexa and tolterodine. Cymbalta is now 30 mg daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the blood pressure pills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We stopped lisinopril and furosemide. You’re only on metoprolol now. Watch for dizziness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your catheter is fine. Keep up with regular changes every few weeks as scheduled with your urologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to keep that appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your code status is DNR/DNI. That’s still correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. No resuscitation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Noted. We’ll make sure all your providers know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared for discharge. You’re alert, stable, and back to baseline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel great. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re going to an extended care facility for a few days. They’ll help with rehab and make sure you’re safe before going home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I understand.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep using the eye gel until it’s done. Use the triamcinolone cream as needed for your face.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Follow up with your new doctor, neurology, and urology. Call if you have fever, confusion, or catheter issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, Mr. ___.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted with altered mental status and tremors following a recent hospital discharge. Initial evaluation revealed no acute intracranial pathology, infection, or metabolic derangement. His confusion was attributed to delirium, likely exacerbated by medications including tolterodine and Celexa, which were discontinued. His myoclonic tremors were managed with an increase in Cymbalta and adjustment of trazodone. A positive urinalysis was determined to reflect colonization due to his chronic indwelling catheter, not infection, so antibiotics were avoided. Conjunctivitis and seborrheic dermatitis improved with targeted treatment. His blood pressure remained low, prompting discontinuation of lisinopril and furosemide. He regained baseline mental status, was stabilized on revised medications, and was discharged to extended care for rehabilitation with follow-up arranged in neurology, urology, and primary care.
